module_title: Making Incense: Sticks, Cones, and Resins

lessons.title: Rolling Incense Sticks with Bamboo and Charcoal
lessons.body: To make incense sticks, you need bamboo sticks (also called blanks), charcoal powder, a binder like gum arabic or makko powder, and your fragrance oil. Bamboo sticks come in lengths of 20-30 cm and thicknesses of 1.5-3 mm. For a beginner batch, start with 100 sticks. You will also need a flat tray or board, a small bowl, and a drying rack. Charcoal powder is the base that carries the scent. It is lightweight and burns steadily. Mix 50 grams of charcoal powder with 10 grams of gum arabic powder (or 15 grams of makko). Add 30-40 ml of water slowly while stirring until you get a thick paste like peanut butter. Let it sit for 10 minutes. If it is too dry, add a little water; if too wet, add a bit more charcoal. Now hold a bamboo stick at one end and dip the other end into the paste, or lay sticks on a tray and spread the paste along the top 10-12 cm with your fingers. Roll the stick between your palms to make an even coating about 2-3 mm thick. Place the coated sticks on a drying rack, with the coated end hanging over the edge. Let them dry in a shaded, well-ventilated area for 24-48 hours. Once dry, you can dip them in fragrance oil or dissolve oil in alcohol and dip. For a stronger scent, mix 5-10 ml of fragrance oil into the paste before coating. In Africa, many makers use locally sourced bamboo and charcoal from cassava or maize cobs. This reduces cost. Test burn a few sticks to check for even burning and scent throw. Adjust binder or oil as needed.

lessons.title: Molding Incense Cones with Natural Binders
lessons.body: Incense cones are easy to make and burn well. You need fine charcoal powder, a natural binder like gum arabic, guar gum, or makko (a traditional Japanese binder made from tabu no ki bark), and fragrance oil. For a small batch, mix 40 grams of charcoal powder with 8 grams of binder. Add 25-30 ml of water gradually until you get a moldable dough that holds its shape but is not sticky. If you want to add fragrance, mix 3-5 ml of oil into the water before adding. Knead the dough for 2-3 minutes. Take a small amount, about the size of a large marble (10-15 grams), and roll it into a ball. Then shape it into a cone by rolling between your palms and pressing the base flat. You can also use a small cone mold, which you can make from clay or buy online. Press the dough firmly into the mold, then tap it out. Place cones on a tray lined with parchment paper. Let them dry in a cool, shaded place for 3-5 days. They are dry when they feel hard and lightweight. If they crack, the dough was too dry; if they sag, too wet. In Africa, you can use cassava starch or plantain peel ash as a binder alternative. Cones burn from the tip down, releasing scent. Test one cone: it should burn for 20-30 minutes. Adjust binder if it goes out. Store dried cones in an airtight container away from moisture.

lessons.title: Burning Resins Directly on Charcoal
lessons.body: Burning resins like frankincense, myrrh, copal, and benzoin is one of the oldest incense methods. You need a heat-resistant bowl or censer, charcoal discs (also called charcoal tablets), and resin tears or powder. Charcoal discs are available in local markets or from suppliers. Light a charcoal disc with a match or lighter. Hold it with tongs until it stops sparking and turns grey, about 2-3 minutes. Place it in the bowl. Sprinkle a small amount of resin (about 1/2 to 1 teaspoon) on top. The resin will melt and release fragrant smoke. Do not use too much at once or it will smother the charcoal. Add more resin as needed. For a longer burn, use a larger charcoal disc. In Africa, you can find resins like frankincense from Ethiopia, myrrh from Somalia, and copal from Madagascar. You can also use locally available resins like gum arabic or dammar. To make a blend, mix resins with a pinch of sandalwood powder or dried herbs. Always burn in a well-ventilated area. Keep away from children and pets. Clean the bowl after each use by scraping off hardened resin. This method is popular for ceremonies, meditation, and masking odors. It requires no binders or rolling, making it perfect for beginners.

lessons.title: Adding Fragrance Oils to Incense Bases
lessons.body: Fragrance oils give incense its scent. You can add them to charcoal paste, resin blends, or directly onto finished sticks and cones. For sticks and cones, the best time to add oil is during mixing. Use 5-10 ml of fragrance oil per 100 grams of dry base. If you add too little, the scent will be weak; too much, and the incense will be oily and burn poorly. Mix the oil with a small amount of alcohol (like vodka or perfumer's alcohol) to help it blend evenly. For 100 grams of base, mix 5 ml oil with 5 ml alcohol, then add to the paste. For dipping finished sticks, dissolve 10 ml of oil in 20 ml of alcohol, dip the coated sticks for 10 seconds, and let dry. You can also make a concentrated oil blend by mixing essential oils or fragrance oils with a carrier oil like jojoba or sweet almond. In Africa, you can use locally available oils like lemongrass, eucalyptus, or shea butter oil. Always test a small batch first. Some oils are stronger than others; citrus oils fade quickly, while patchouli and sandalwood last longer. Store oils in dark glass bottles away from heat. When blending, start with a base note (like sandalwood), a middle note (like lavender), and a top note (like orange). This creates a balanced scent. Keep records of your recipes so you can repeat successful blends.

lessons.title: Drying and Curing Incense for Best Burn
lessons.body: Drying and curing are critical for good incense. If incense is not fully dry, it will not burn evenly and may go out. After rolling sticks or molding cones, place them on a drying rack in a shaded, well-ventilated area. Direct sunlight can cause cracking and fade the scent. For sticks, hang them with the coated end down or lay them flat on parchment paper. For cones, place them upright. The drying time depends on humidity. In dry climates, sticks take 24-48 hours; cones take 3-5 days. In humid climates, it can take twice as long. You can use a fan to speed drying, but keep it on low. Once surface-dry, move to curing. Curing allows the scent to deepen and the binder to fully set. Place dried incense in an airtight container, like a glass jar or plastic tub, and store in a cool, dark place. For sticks, cure for 1-2 weeks; cones for 2-3 weeks. Some makers cure for a month for premium quality. During curing, check occasionally for mold. If mold appears, discard the batch. After curing, test burn a piece. It should burn from end to end without going out, and the scent should be rich. If it burns too fast, the binder may be too low; if it keeps going out, the incense may be too damp or the binder too high. Adjust your next batch accordingly. Proper drying and curing make a big difference in quality and customer satisfaction.

lessons.title: Packaging Incense for Sale in Local Markets
lessons.body: Packaging protects your incense and makes it attractive to buyers. For local markets, simple and affordable packaging works best. You can use small clear plastic bags, paper envelopes, or cardboard tubes. For sticks, bundle 10-20 sticks together and wrap them in a paper band or tie with raffia. For cones, place 6-10 cones in a small bag or box. Label each package with the scent name, quantity, and your contact. In Africa, you can use locally sourced materials like banana leaves, woven grass, or recycled paper. For a professional look, print labels with your brand name and a simple logo. Include burning instructions: "Light tip, blow out flame, place in heatproof holder." Price your incense based on cost of materials and labor. A common markup is 2-3 times the cost. For example, if a pack costs 500 CFA to make, sell for 1000-1500 CFA. Sell at local markets, shops, or online via WhatsApp or Facebook. Offer testers so customers can smell the scent. Keep packaging airtight to preserve scent. Store in a cool, dry place. You can also create gift sets with 3-4 different scents. As you grow, consider eco-friendly packaging like biodegradable bags or recycled paper. Always comply with local regulations for labeling. Good packaging builds trust and repeat customers.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Making Incense â Sticks, Cones, and Resins

Incense is one of the oldest value-added products in African agribusiness. From the frankincense and myrrh trade routes of the Horn of Africa to the resin-rich woodlands of Namibia and the spice markets of Zanzibar, aromatic materials have moved through African hands for millennia. Today, a small producer in Kumasi, Mombasa, or Lilongwe can turn locally sourced resins, gums, charcoal, and fragrance oils into a shelf-ready product with modest equipment and strong margins. This Practical Reference consolidates the six core lessons in this module â rolling sticks, molding cones, burning resins, adding fragrance oils, drying and curing, and packaging â into one working document you can print and keep at the production bench.

Treat this as a business document, not a craft hobby sheet. Every technical choice below has a cost, a yield, and a market consequence. Read the numbers, then run your own trials.

Lesson 1 â Rolling Incense Sticks with Bamboo and Charcoal

The bamboo-core method is the most commercially scalable format in Africa because bamboo skewers are cheap, widely available, and produce a uniform product. The base is a blend of charcoal powder (for clean, even burn), a binder such as gum arabic or gum tragacanth, and water. A typical working base for 1 kg of dry mix:

Table 1 â Standard charcoal stick base (per 1 kg dry mix)
IngredientShareWeightFunctionLocal sourcing note
Charcoal powder (hardwood)55%550 gBurn fuel, neutral baseSource from local charcoal burners; sieve to 200 mesh
Gum arabic (acacia)15%150 gBinderSahel gum arabic; Sudan, Niger, Senegal
Wood powder (sandalwood or local substitute)20%200 gBody, burn modifierUse sawmill fines; avoid treated timber
Fragrance oil or resin extract8%80 gScentImport or locally distilled (e.g., lemongrass, eucalyptus)
Potassium nitrate (optional)2%20 gBurn enhancerAgricultural grade; use sparingly

Source: Proportions adapted from Neal (2003) and from technical notes in FAO's Non-Wood Forest Products 1: Flavours and Fragrances of Plant Origin (1995).

Mix dry ingredients first, then add water slowly until the paste holds a shape without cracking. Roll the paste onto pre-soaked bamboo sticks (soak at least 30 minutes to prevent cracking during drying). Roll on a flat glass or plastic sheet. Aim for 2â3 mm thickness. Lay sticks horizontally on a drying rack.

Lesson 2 â Molding Incense Cones with Natural Binders

Cones are a premium format and command higher unit prices in urban markets and export. The base is similar to sticks but with a higher binder ratio (18â22%) and no bamboo core. Use a small cone mold or hand-roll into a cone shape. Key binders available in Africa:

Table 2 â Natural binders for cone and stick incense
BinderOriginWorking ratioBurn characterCost signal
Gum arabicAcacia senegal / seyal (Sahel)12â18%Clean, slow, low ashLowâmedium
Gum tragacanthAstragalus spp. (Iran, Turkey)8â12%Strong, flexible, premiumHigh
Gum karayaSterculia urens (India, West Africa)10â15%Thick paste, good mold releaseMedium
Cassava starchManihot esculenta (sub-Saharan Africa)15â20%Cheap, but can smokeVery low
Xanthan gumFermentation (imported)2â4%Strong gel, tricky dryingMediumâhigh

Source: Binder properties compiled from FAO NWFP 1 (1995) and from the Gums and Resins Handbook published by the Centre for the Development of Industry (CDI, now ACP Business Climate) technical notes.

Lesson 3 â Burning Resins Directly on Charcoal

Resin incense â frankincense (Boswellia), myrrh (Commiphora), opopanax, and African copal â is the highest-margin product per gram because it needs almost no processing. You sell the resin as-is or blended. To demonstrate at market, place a lit charcoal disc inside a heat-proof bowl, add a small pinch of resin, and let the smoke rise. Do not powder the resin too finely; pea-sized pieces give a longer, more controlled burn. This format is especially strong in markets where customers already know frankincense or myrrh by name.

â  SAFETY WARNING â READ BEFORE PRODUCTION
  • Ventilation is mandatory. Charcoal combustion produces carbon monoxide. Never burn charcoal or cure large batches in a closed room, bedroom, or vehicle. Work outdoors or under forced-air extraction.
  • Fragrance oils are concentrates. Wear nitrile gloves and eye protection when handling. Do not ingest. Keep away from children and open flames during mixing.
  • Potassium nitrate is an oxidizer. Store separately from fuels, in a dry, locked cabinet. Do not grind it with other ingredients.
  • Fire risk during curing. Resin-rich and oil-rich incense can self-heat. Cure in a cool, shaded, ventilated area â never in direct sun or near a heat source.
  • Respiratory protection. Wear a dust mask when sieving charcoal and wood powders. Fine charcoal dust is a known respiratory irritant.

Lesson 4 â Adding Fragrance Oils to Incense Bases

Fragrance load is the single biggest driver of scent throw and cost. The industry benchmark for dipped or mixed incense is 5â12% fragrance oil by weight of dry base. Below 5% the scent fades in storage; above 12% the product becomes oily, slow to dry, and expensive. For resin blends, 3â8% is usually enough because the resin carries its own aroma. Always dilute fragrance oil in a small amount of a carrier (dipropylene glycol or a neutral alcohol) before mixing into the paste â this distributes the scent evenly and prevents "hot spots" that smell burnt.

Africa-specific opportunity: use locally distilled essential oils â lemongrass, eucalyptus, clove, cinnamon, hibiscus, and baobab â as the top note, and use imported synthetic accords only to fix and extend the scent. This lowers import cost and gives you a genuine origin story for export buyers.

Lesson 5 â Drying and Curing Incense for Best Burn

Drying and curing are two different stages and both are non-negotiable.

  • Drying (24â72 hours): Lay sticks or cones on a mesh rack in a shaded, ventilated space. Turn once after 12 hours. Do not use direct sun â it cracks the surface and drives off the fragrance.
  • Curing (2â4 weeks): Once surface-dry, pack loosely in an airtight container or lined carton. This allows moisture to equalize and the fragrance to bind into the base. Cured incense burns slower, smells fuller, and resists mold.

Test burn a sample from each batch before packing. A good stick should light easily, hold a steady ember, produce a thin white smoke, and leave a short grey ash. If it goes out, the binder ratio is too low or the product is still damp. If it burns too fast and smells sharp, the charcoal or nitrate ratio is too high.

Lesson 6 â Packaging Incense for Sale in Local Markets

Packaging is where small producers lose margin. Keep it simple, consistent, and branded.

  • Sticks: bundle 20â25 sticks in a paper sleeve or cellophane tube with a printed label. Add a batch code and a "made in [country]" line.
  • Cones: pack 10â12 cones in a small box or tin. Cones travel better than sticks for export.
  • Resins: sell in 50 g and 100 g sealed pouches with a clear window so the customer sees the grade.
  • Label essentials: product name, format, net weight, fragrance, burn time, batch number, producer contact, and a safety line ("burn on heat-proof surface, keep away from children").

Price for value, not for weight. A well-cured, well-packaged 20-stick sleeve can sell at 2â3Ã the price of an unbranded bundle in the same market. In tourist and export channels, add a short origin card explaining the resin or botanical source â buyers pay for the story.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Weigh every ingredient â eyeballing causes batch-to-batch inconsistency and customer complaints.
  2. Sieve charcoal and wood powders to 200 mesh before mixing.
  3. Soak bamboo sticks at least 30 minutes before rolling.
  4. Keep fragrance oil load between 5â12% (sticks/cones) and 3â8% (resins).
  5. Dry in shade with airflow for 24â72 hours; never in direct sun.
  6. Cure sealed for 2â4 weeks before packaging.
  7. Test-burn one sample per batch and record the result.
  8. Label every unit with batch code, weight, and safety line before it leaves the bench.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Non-Wood Forest Products 1: Flavours and Fragrances of Plant Origin (free full text; covers gums, resins, and essential oils).
  • FAO â Non-Wood Forest Products 2: Gum Arabic (free; binder sourcing and trade data).
  • FAO â Non-Wood Forest Products 9: Commodity and Trade Data (free; market sizing for aromatics).
  • UNIDO â Agro-processing and SME development resources (free technical and business guides).
  • ILO â Occupational safety guidance for small workshops (free; ventilation and dust control).

Business note: Start with one format â usually sticks â master the burn and scent, then add cones and resins as your market and cash flow allow. Record every batch: date, recipe, yield, cost, and test-burn result. After twenty batches you will have a proprietary formula and a defensible price. That is the difference between a hobby and an agribusiness.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of charcoal powder in incense sticks?
options: B) To act as a binder
C) To serve as a burnable base
quiz.explanation: Charcoal powder is the base that burns and carries the fragrance.

quiz.q: Which binder is commonly used for making incense cones?
quiz.explanation: Gum arabic is a natural binder that holds the cone together.

quiz.q: How long should you let incense sticks dry before curing?
quiz.explanation: Sticks need 24-48 hours to dry in a shaded, ventilated area.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to burn resin directly?
quiz.explanation: Resins are burned on a lit charcoal disc to release fragrance.

quiz.q: How much fragrance oil should you add to 100g of incense base?
quiz.explanation: 5-10 ml of oil per 100g gives a good scent without making it oily.

quiz.q: Why is curing incense important?
options: A) It makes it dry faster
B) It deepens the scent and sets the binder
D) It makes it burn faster
quiz.explanation: Curing allows the scent to mature and the binder to fully harden.

quiz.q: What is a good packaging material for incense in local markets?
quiz.explanation: Clear plastic bags are affordable and show the product.

quiz.q: What happens if incense is not fully dry before burning?
quiz.explanation: Damp incense will not burn evenly and often goes out.

quiz.q: Which of these is a natural binder used in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Cassava starch can be used as a binder in some African incense recipes.

quiz.q: How long should you cure incense cones?
quiz.explanation: Cones are typically cured for 2-3 weeks for best results.

quiz.q: What is the first step in rolling incense sticks?
quiz.explanation: You must first mix the charcoal powder with a binder and water to make a paste.

quiz.q: What is a common resin from Ethiopia?
quiz.explanation: Frankincense is a well-known resin from Ethiopia.

quiz.q: How can you test if incense cones are dry?
options: A) They feel hard and lightweight
quiz.explanation: Dry cones are hard and lightweight; if soft, they need more drying.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding alcohol when mixing fragrance oil?
options: A) To make it burn faster
B) To help oil blend evenly
quiz.explanation: Alcohol helps the oil mix uniformly with the base.

quiz.q: Which scent note is considered a base note?
quiz.explanation: Sandalwood is a base note that lasts longer in incense.

quiz.q: What is a good markup for pricing incense?
quiz.explanation: A markup of 2-3 times the cost is common for handmade products.

quiz.q: What should you do if your incense sticks keep going out?
options: B) Add more binder or dry longer
quiz.explanation: Going out often means too much moisture or too little binder.

quiz.q: Which of these is a top note in perfumery?
quiz.explanation: Orange is a top note that evaporates quickly.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store dried incense?
options: A) In an airtight container in a cool, dark place
quiz.explanation: Airtight, cool, dark storage preserves scent and prevents mold.

quiz.q: How many grams of charcoal powder are suggested for a beginner batch of 100 sticks?
quiz.explanation: 50 grams of charcoal powder is enough for about 100 sticks.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when adding fragrance oil?
quiz.explanation: Too little gives weak scent; too much makes incense oily and burn poorly.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a drying rack?
options: A) To keep incense off surfaces and allow air circulation
B) To make incense dry faster in sun
quiz.explanation: A rack allows air to circulate around the incense for even drying.

quiz.q: Which of these is a local material for packaging in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Banana leaves are a natural, biodegradable packaging option.

quiz.q: How long should you knead the dough for cones?
quiz.explanation: Kneading for 2-3 minutes ensures even mixing.

quiz.q: What is a sign that incense cones are too wet?
quiz.explanation: If cones sag, the dough has too much water.

quiz.q: Which resin is commonly used in incense and comes from Somalia?
quiz.explanation: Myrrh is a resin from Somalia and other parts of Africa.

quiz.q: What should you do before burning resin on charcoal?
options: B) Light the charcoal until it is grey
quiz.explanation: Charcoal must be fully lit and grey before adding resin.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test a new incense recipe?
options: D) Store it for a year
quiz.explanation: Always test burn a small sample to check burn and scent.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid direct sunlight when drying incense?
options: B) It causes cracking and fades scent
quiz.explanation: Direct sun can crack the incense and degrade the fragrance.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of curing incense for a month?
options: B) It develops a richer scent
quiz.explanation: Longer curing allows the scent to deepen and mature.
